newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Chan latest victim of fight for Bougainville riches.
newsitem.headline: Chan latest victim of fight for Bougainville riches.

text.p: Without one shot fired in anger, the small Papua New Guinea army on Wednesday forced prime minister Sir Julius Chan out of office over a failed plan to bring mercenaries into the South Pacific.
In agreeing to stand aside, Chan became the latest victim of the nine-year secessionist conflict on the resource-rich Bougainville island.

"It may have looked very cold-blooded at times but a developing country has to take very tough decisions at times," Chan, after stepping aside, told a news conference of his decision to hire mercenaries to put down the island rebellion.
Chan told parliament on Wednesday that he and his deputy and defence minister would immediately relinquish their posts in order to defuse an "explosive situation".
Overnight heavily armed soldiers and thousands of anti-government protesters had staged a sit-in around parliament, trapping more than 100 politicians and staff inside.

Chan had escaped an initial call in parliament on Tuesday to stand down. His defiance then of a rebellious army, opposition and government politicians and thousands on the street risked igniting a powder keg of resentment in the capital Port Moresby.
Last week Port Moresby was scarred by two days of looting and violence as sacked army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok led his men in defiance of the prime minister.
Singirok had called on Chan to resign over the hiring of 70 African mercenaries from the British-based military consultancy Sandline International. Singirok was promptly sacked.
Singirok said the use of mercenaries to end fighting in Bougainville was morally wrong as it would lead to the deaths of many civilians.
The conflict has already left thousands dead, either from fighting or a lack of medical facilities due to a blockade of the island, 800 km (500 miles) north-east of Port Moresby.
But on Wednesday it was Chan who became the latest casualty from the intractable war on Bougainville, the longest-running armed conflict in the South Pacific.

Port Moresby has failed to solve the Bougainville question, despite 13 rounds of peace talks, numerous military offensives and billions of dollars in military costs and lost revenues -- but the prize is rich for whoever finds a solution.
The giant Panguna copper mine, owned by Anglo-Australian mining giant RTZ-CRA Ltd, was generating a third of Papua New Guinea's foreign exchange before it was forced to close by rebels in 1989.
Solving Bougainville would also boost Papua New Guinea's international reputation among resource investors.

Papua New Guinea has huge resources of gold, oil and copper, but it has a track record of problems with landowners, the most public being the big Ok Tedi gold/copper mine, controlled by The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd of Australia, and Bougainville.

The concept of mineral rights is alien in a country where sorcery and cults co-exist with Christianity, where its 4.3 million people speak 700 languages and some remote villages are run under ancient traditions.
Chan said the other factor that led him to step aside was a fear that Papua New Guinea faced economic chaos as a result of the worst political crisis since independence in 1975.

Papua New Guinea has only just recovered from an economic slide which saw rapid growth at the start of the 1990s collapse in just a few years, falling from 16.6 percent in 1993 to 2.4 percent in 1994. The economy showed a moderate growth rate of around 2.3 percent in 1996.
But Papua New Guinea has a reputation for political, economic and social instability.

Since independence from Australia in 1975, various governments have struggled to instill a national ethos. Politicians have failed to create a binding party system and party allegiances are bought and sold.
Papua New Guinea is also a nation scarred by tribal wars, where the law of the land is "payback" and where gangs called "rascals" stage gun battles with police in the streets.
Port Moresby is under a 10.00 p.m. to 4.00 a.m. curfew in an attempt to curb crime and residents, rich and poor, live behind security fences crowned with razor wire.
Chan's decision to step aside on Wednesday doused the flames of civil unrest which were threatening to engulf Port Moresby and possibly the rest of the country.
"The only thing I plead now is please bring order back," Chan said.
